passage: Halfway through the month, Afreen laid her plan beside her progress chart on the study table and counted. Four chapters behind. Her first thought was to sit up later. Instead she pulled out the last six years of papers and marked which topics turned up in every one: probability, matrices, integration. Two chapters had appeared only once. The next day she showed her list to Ojas Sir after class. He read it, tapped one chapter, and said, "Leave these two. But keep this one, it comes as a short question." That evening Afreen crossed out the two chapters, moved their hours to probability and matrices, and rewrote the week. The gap did not vanish, but for the first time the calendar looked possible.

qa.q: How many chapters was Afreen behind at the halfway point?

qa.a: Afreen felt relieved and hopeful, because the cuts turned a worrying gap into a plan that fits the days left. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could protect Afreen against a surprise question from a dropped chapter, and why?
qa.a: Afreen could keep one-page summaries of the dropped chapters to skim in the last week, since a short read costs little time.

"Ma'am, can I show you something?" Rajni held out her planner. "It's the fifteenth. I was supposed to have finished twelve chapters. I've done eight."
Avni Ma'am looked at it. "Four behind. What's left?"
"Coordination compounds, polymers, everyday chemistry, surface chemistry, and the big ones, electrochemistry and kinetics."
"Have you looked at the last ten papers?"
"Yes. Electrochemistry and kinetics come every year. Polymers and everyday chemistry are a few marks, and hardly ever asked."
"So what do you want to do?"
Rajni took a breath. "Drop polymers and everyday chemistry for now. Put those hours into electrochemistry and kinetics. Is that okay?"
"It's a sensible trade. Read their summaries once at the end if you have time."
Rajni crossed two lines off the planner. "I feel less behind already."

qa.q: How many chapters had Rajni done by the fifteenth?
What does Rajni's deep breath suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous about asking to drop topics, worried it might sound like giving up.

qa.q: Why is dropping polymers and everyday chemistry a good trade?
qa.a: They carry few marks and are rarely asked, while electrochemistry and kinetics come every year, so the hours earn more there.

qa.q: How does Avni Ma'am see Rajni's plan?
qa.a: She sees it as sensible and agrees, adding that the dropped summaries can be read once if time allows.

grounding: A dialogue shows a student at the halfway check, four chapters behind, dropping rarely asked topics with the teacher's agreement.

passage: I'm Aparna, and halfway through my last month before boards I opened my planner and felt sick. Fifteen days gone, and I was four chapters behind in History. My first thought was to study till two every night and catch up. Instead my cousin Preeti, who had sat the same exam, made me open the past papers. We went through ten years together. Two of my remaining chapters, on world history and a minor dynasty, had come up only twice in ten years. The chapters on the national movement came up every single year. The next day I asked Sir if I could leave those two for the end. He said yes. I moved all their hours to the national movement. Papa passed my room that night and said, "Sleeping at a normal time, beti? Good."

qa.q: How many chapters behind was Aparna?
What did Aparna feel on opening the planner at the halfway mark?
qa.a: She felt sick with worry, seeing she was four chapters behind.

qa.q: Why ask the teacher before dropping the chapters?
qa.a: The teacher can confirm the chapters really are low-yield, so she drops them with confidence instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Papa feel seeing her sleep at a normal time?
qa.a: Papa seems relieved and approving, glad she isn't cramming late into the night.

grounding: A student recalls being four chapters behind at the halfway point and, with the teacher's agreement, moving time from rarely asked topics to ones in every paper.
